title: Lakotokoto
author: Laker Grace
desc: Unroasted sesame ground coarse, pressed with hot water to draw the oil out, rolled into balls and dropped into boiling water — named, people think, for the sound it makes as it cooks.
longDesc: Lakotokoto is made from ground unroasted simsim, which makes it quite different from odii and from everything else in the northern repertoire. It stands alongside dek ngor, boo and malakwang as a dish that has stood the test of time in Acholi. The processing is the craft: grind coarse but not to a paste, pour hot water on and press to release the oil, then roll the pressed simsim into balls. The name is thought to come from the sound it makes in the pot.
ingredients: Unroasted simsim (sesame) — no quantities are given in the source
Boiled dry fish, or beef or offal cooked separately
The lakotokoto oil, or any cooking oil
equipment: Mortar and pestle, grinding stone, or a grinder
steps: // Choosing the simsim
Look for fresh clean simsim, or wash it clean to remove the bitter taste.
Some cooks pound it slightly and thresh it to remove the outer shells by winnowing, which is credited for a whitish look in the finished dish rather than a blackish one.
// Grinding
Grind it, on a grinding machine or a traditional grinding stone.
Grind it only slightly, so it does not turn completely into a paste, but enough to remove the visible tiny particles of seed.
// Pressing out the oil
Boil water for pressing the ground simsim.
Pour the hot water onto the ground simsim, carefully and in balanced proportion, so the lump is not overwhelmed by water. Hot water rather than cold is used because it eases the pressing.
Press the lump until it is clear of oil, and pour the oil off into a separate container.
// Shaping
Roll the pressed simsim into small balls and spread them in a container, ready for cooking.
Some cooks mix the ground simsim with soda ash or magadi to keep the taste and keep it fresh.
// Cooking
Boil water, then add your chosen ingredients — onions and tomatoes for boiled lakotokoto.
Or, to fry it, fry the onions and tomatoes in the lakotokoto oil or any cooking oil.
Pour the lump of ground lakotokoto slowly into the boiling water.
After about 20 minutes, add salt.
Keep the water just sufficient so it does not burn.
Leave it cooking at least an hour, covered so it steams and keeps its aroma.
Serve with kwon kal or kalo, sweet potatoes, or cassava flour dough.
chefTips: Grind it only slightly. Ground to a paste you have sesame butter, not lakotokoto — the coarseness is the dish.
Hot water for the pressing, not cold. It eases the process of pressing the oil out, which is the stated reason.
Taste the simsim before you buy it. Bitterness in the seed carries straight through, and the people who cook this professionally say so.

There are two incompatible techniques in the one good source and neither is wrong. One cook presses the oil out and separates it off completely; another presses only slightly and does not separate it at all, arguing that keeping the oil prevents the dish becoming bitter. Both are recorded.
Twenty minutes before the salt, then at least an hour of cooking. It is a slow dish.
Keep the water sufficient but no more. Too much and it will not thicken; too little and it burns.
Cover it as it steams, to retain the aroma.
The name is thought to come from the sound the food makes as it cooks — la-ko-to-ko-to. Nobody has established that, but everybody says it.
No quantities are given anywhere in the source. Nothing here is estimated to cover that.
commonMistakes: Buying bitter simsim without tasting it.
Adding the salt at the start.
Adding too much water so it never comes together.
sources: Adapted from 'Lakotokoto: It's taste depends on additional ingredients', Daily Monitor, 20 October 2012, updated 9 January 2021, bylined only as an email address that the page redacts — the selection, washing, slight pounding and winnowing, the grind-only-slightly instruction, the hot-water pressing and its stated reason, the rolling into balls, the soda ash or magadi option, the 20-minutes-then-salt timing and the at-least-an-hour covered cook are all from that article.

It names three practitioners and records a genuine disagreement between two of them, which is reproduced rather than reconciled: Ventorino Akumu, 57, presses the oil out and separates it off; Evaline Achora of Montana Hotel, Gulu, presses only slightly and does not separate the oil, arguing it prevents the dish becoming bitter. Goretti Akullo of Binen Restaurant, Gulu, advises tasting the simsim at market to avoid bitterness.
That article gives no ingredient list and no quantities at all. None has been estimated.
The etymology from the sound the food makes as it cooks, and its standing alongside dek ngor, boo and malakwang as an Acholi dish that has stood the test of time, are from the same source.
reheating: Warm gently with a little water.
healthBenefits: Sesame is one of the richest plant sources of calcium, plus magnesium, iron and zinc.
High in plant protein and in lignans.
Pressing the oil out reduces the fat considerably, which is one reason the two techniques give different dishes.
Naturally free of gluten and dairy.
culturalNote: Unroasted sesame is the unusual thing here — northern Uganda roasts simsim for almost everything else, and odii, the signature condiment, is roasted sesame and groundnut pounded together. That lakotokoto goes the other way, and presses the oil out rather than keeping it in, makes it the most technically distinctive dish in the region.
